t: Longest Happy Prefix — KMP Failure Function, Z-Algorithm, and Rolling Hash
o: We need the longest proper prefix of `s` that is also a suffix of `s` (they may overlap). For "level" the only such string is "l"; for "ababab" it is "abab" since prefix/suffix may overlap. With n up to 1e5, any O(n²) comparison of all candidate prefixes against suffixes is too slow in the worst case (e.g. "aaaa...a"), so we need a linear-time string structure: the KMP failure function, the Z-array, or a polynomial rolling hash. All three answer the question by looking at a single precomputed array/hash value at position n-1.
k: The answer's length equals the failure function value f[n-1] from KMP, or z[n-1] from the Z-array computed on s itself.
A rolling hash lets us compare prefix and suffix hashes in O(1); using two different moduli/base pairs makes collisions astronomically unlikely.
All optimal approaches are O(n) time and O(n) space.

a.i: Try every length L from n-1 down to 1 and directly compare s[0..L-1] with s[n-L..n-1]. This is the most direct translation of the definition. It passes small inputs but degrades to O(n²) on strings like "aaaa...a", so it is only for building intuition.
s: For L from n-1 down to 1:
Compare s.substring(0, L) with s.substring(n - L).
a.t: O(n²) worst case — up to n candidate lengths, each compared in O(n).
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond output slicing (implementation-dependent).

a.i: The KMP failure function f[i] stores the length of the longest proper prefix of s[0..i] that is also its suffix. By definition this is exactly what we want at i = n-1. Build f with the standard two-pointer recurrence: while mismatched, fall back to f[j-1]; on match, extend j.
s: Initialize f array of size n and pointer j = 0.
For i from 1 to n-1: while j > 0 and s[i] != s[j], set j = f[j-1].
a.t: O(n) — j increases at most once per iteration and each fallback strictly decreases it, amortizing to linear total work.

a.i: Precompute prefix hashes so the hash of any substring is obtained in O(1): hash(s[l..r]) = (h[r+1] - h[l]*p^(r-l+1)) mod M. The prefix of length L matches the suffix of length L iff their hashes are equal. A single modulus risks collisions under adversarial tests, so use two independent (base, mod) pairs and require both to match.
s: Pick two base/modulus pairs (e.g. base 131 mod ~2^61 or large primes).
Compute forward prefix hashes h1, h2 and powers p1, p2.
For L from n-1 down to 1, compute hash of s[0..L-1] and of s[n-L..n-1] for both pairs.
If both pairs match, return s.substring(0, L).

c.python:
class Solution:
    def longestPrefix(self, s: str) -> str:
        n = len(s)
        MOD1, MOD2, B1, B2 = 1_000_000_007, 998_244_353, 131, 137
        h1 = h2 = 0
        rh1 = rh2 = 0
        pw1 = pw2 = 1
        ans = 0
        for i in range(n):
            c = ord(s[i])
            h1 = (h1 * B1 + c) % MOD1
            h2 = (h2 * B2 + c) % MOD2
            rh1 = (rh1 + c * pw1) % MOD1
            rh2 = (rh2 + c * pw2) % MOD2
            pw1 = pw1 * B1 % MOD1
            pw2 = pw2 * B2 % MOD2
            if i + 1 < n and h1 == rh1 and h2 == rh2:
                ans = i + 1
        return s[:ans]

a.t: O(n) — one pass computing hashes; each candidate check is O(1).
a.sp: O(1) extra space (hashes kept incrementally), plus the returned substring.

w: In an interview, lead with the KMP failure function: it is deterministic, easy to verify, and shows mastery of a classic technique; mention the rolling hash as an alternative and note the double-hash trick against collisions. Common pitfalls: forgetting the prefix must be *proper* (never return the whole string — note f[n-1] < n automatically, but with hashing you must exclude L = n); off-by-one errors when mapping failure length to substring bounds; single-modulus hashing being hackable. Edge cases: all-equal characters like "aaaa" (answer "aaa"), no happy prefix like "abcd" (answer ""), and single-character input (answer ""). Likely follow-ups: count all happy prefixes (sum distinct border lengths via the failure chain), find the shortest one, or apply the same idea to repeated substring pattern (LeetCode 459).
